title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADR Process
author: Alex Kim
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's authoritative architecture and engineering standards covering API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving requirements, observability, performance targets, and the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process. It is intended for engineers, tech leads, and architects making changes to platform services and public APIs.

Principles (applies to all sections)
- Developer-first: prioritize clear, discoverable contracts and reproducible developer workflows.
- Observable & debuggable: every service change must be measurable through metrics, traces, and logs.
- Production-safe by default: safe rollouts, automated fallbacks, and tested rollback plans.
- Cost- and performance-aware: engineering trade-offs must include unit-cost, latency, and reliability implications.
- Ownership & lifecycle: a named owning team for every service, model, and dashboard.

1) API standards
Intro: All public and internal HTTP/GRPC APIs must follow this section to ensure consistency and interoperability.

1.1 Surface and formats
- Primary API: JSON over HTTPS (REST) and gRPC for high-throughput internal RPCs.
- Use OpenAPI (v3) for REST endpoints and proto3 for gRPC with service and message documentation.
- All APIs must publish a machine-readable schema in the service repo: /api/openapi.yaml or /api/service.proto.

1.2 Versioning
- Semantic versioning of public APIs: v1, v2 as path prefix (/v1/...).
- Backwards-incompatible changes require an ADR and a deprecation timeline (>= 90 days) for hosted APIs.
- Minor/patch changes should not require breaking clients and must be deployed behind feature flags where possible.

1.3 Naming and resource modeling
- Use plural resource names (e.g., /models, /deployments).
- Endpoint names should be nouns for resources and verbs for actions when necessary (POST /models/:id/activate).

1.4 Errors and status codes
- Use standard HTTP codes. Provide a JSON error object with fields: code, message, details (optional). Example: {"code": "MODEL_NOT_FOUND", "message": "Model id x not found", "details": [...] }
- For gRPC, map to canonical status codes and include a structured payload in the trailing metadata where appropriate.

1.5 Idempotency and retries
- PUT and DELETE must be idempotent. For non-idempotent POSTs, support an Idempotency-Key header.
- Document retry semantics (which codes can be retried) and provide client libraries with built-in retry/backoff consistent across SDKs.

1.6 Pagination, filtering, and sorting
- Use cursor-based pagination for lists with potentially large result sets. Return next_cursor and has_more.
- Filtering expression: support limited server-side filtering and document queryable fields. Avoid unbounded server-side joins.

1.7 Authentication & authorization
- OAuth2 / Bearer tokens for public API. Mutual TLS and mTLS for sensitive internal control plane endpoints.
- All endpoints must validate scopes and principals; use centralized auth libraries where available.

1.8 Rate limiting & quotas
- Document per-route rate limits in OpenAPI extensions and expose headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

1.9 Documentation & examples
- Each API must include: quickstart, examples for common SDKs, and example error responses. Use the docs site generator to publish.

2) Coding standards
Intro: Keep code readable, testable, and consistent across repos. The goal is fast onboarding and low-cost maintenance.

2.1 Languages & runtime support
- Primary backend languages: Go (services), Python (inference glue, lightweight services), Rust/C++ (performance-critical runtime).
- Use language-specific style guides (gofmt, Black, rustfmt). Enforce via CI.

2.2 Repository layout and packaging
- One service per repository unless tightly coupled. Use mono-repo only when justified with clear ownership.
- Include CONTRIBUTING.md, CODEOWNERS, and a service README with run instructions and health endpoints.

2.3 Testing requirements
- Unit tests with >= 80% coverage for core logic.
- Integration tests for cross-service contracts. Use testcontainers or staging infra for ephemeral integration runs.
- End-to-end smoke tests for critical user journeys (deployment, inference path).

2.4 Code review and PR expectations
- All changes via pull requests with at least one reviewer; large changes require design review and an ADR when altering cross-cutting behavior.
- PRs must include changelog notes if public API/behavior is affected.

2.5 Dependency management
- Record dependencies in lock files. Use automated dependency updates (dependabot or internal tooling) and require staged canary runs for major version bumps.

2.6 Secrets and credentials
- No secrets in VCS. Use the company secrets manager and inject credentials via environment or secret volumes.

3) Infrastructure standards
Intro: Infrastructure as code is required for all long-lived cloud resources. The goal is reproducible deployments and clear cost ownership.

3.1 IaC & repositories
- Terraform is the standard for cloud infra. State is stored in remote backends (Terraform Cloud / S3+Locking).
- CloudFormation/ARM only when provider-native features are required and approved by infra.

3.2 Account & networking model
- Use a multi-account strategy (prod, staging, dev, experiments) with standardized account bootstrap templates.
- VPCs: default CIDR blocks and subnet patterns defined in network catalogue. Use Transit Gateway or VPC Peering per architecture guides.

3.3 CI/CD and deployment patterns
- CI must run unit tests, linting, and build artifacts. CD uses staged pipelines: canary -> regional rollout -> global.
- Automate schema and contract validation for API changes during CI.

3.4 Secrets, KMS, and encryption
- KMS for envelope encryption. Use HSM/KMS integrations for private deployments.
- All data-at-rest must be encrypted using managed keys; access is audited.

3.5 Capacity & cost controls
- Tagging is mandatory (team:, service:, environment:, cost-center:). Daily cost reports and alerts for over-budget trends.

4) Model-serving standards
Intro: These rules apply to models served on Redwood (hosted/dedicated/private). They ensure safe, performant, and debuggable model deployments.

4.1 Model packaging and artifacts
- Each model release includes: model artifact (quantized variants if applicable), model card (metadata), example prompts, eval results (unit and regression), and a deployment manifest.
- Supported artifact formats: ONNX, TorchScript, or framework-specific bundles accepted by the runtime.

4.2 Versioning and lineage
- Every model has a semantic identifier: model-name@version (e.g., redwood-13b@v1.2.0). Store lineage and provenance (training dataset hashes, tokenizer version, quantization steps) in the model registry.

4.3 Quantization and performance profiles
- Publish quantization profiles (e.g., int8, int4) and expected perf characteristics (p50 latency, throughput at batch size N, memory). Attach to model card.

4.4 Rollouts and canaries
- Use phased rollouts: internal -> beta customers -> general availability. Canary traffic must be isolated with traffic shadowing and monitored for quality regressions.
- Automatic rollback policy: trigger on SLO breaches (latency or error-rate) or quality regressions flagged by evals.

4.5 Caching and KV management
- Runtime must support prefix caching, KV cache exports/imports for warm starts, and caching policies (TTL, size). Document cache invalidation strategy per deployment.

4.6 Safety and evaluation
- Every model must pass safety scans (toxicity classifiers, PII leakage tests) and regression test suites tied to known prompt-sets before public rollout.

4.7 Telemetry & debugging hooks
- Model-level metrics: per-model p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens per second, inference error rate, cache hit ratio, and quality score derived from evals.
- Provide sample traces that include model variant, quantization profile, and routing decision.

5) Observability standards
Intro: Observability is essential for operating a multi-tenant inference platform. Instrumentation must be consistent and actionable.

5.1 Metrics
- Use Prometheus-style naming: <service>_<component>_<metric>_{total|seconds|ratio}. Example: inference_request_duration_seconds_bucket.
- Cardinality: avoid high-cardinality labels except where necessary (use hashed ids or sampled traces).
- Required baseline metrics: request_count, request_error_count, request_duration_seconds (histogram), cache_hit_ratio, gpu_utilization, queue_depth.

5.2 Tracing
- Use distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry. Traces must propagate request IDs and include model variant, routing decision, and cache interaction spans.

5.3 Logs
- Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, service, level, request_id, user_id (hashed), message, and debug_context (optional).
- Log retention and sensitive data rules: PII must be redacted before logs are persisted in long-term storage.

5.4 Dashboards & alerts
- Standard dashboards: per-service overview, per-model inference health, and per-region capacity.
- Alerting thresholds should map to SLOs and runbook actions. Use alert fatigue controls (grouping, deduplication, paging thresholds).

5.5 SLOs and error budgets
- Every customer-facing service must have SLOs defined and published in the service README and in the SLO registry. Example SLOs (see Performance section).

6) Performance standards
Intro: Performance expectations differ by product surface (hosted API, dedicated, private). Use this section for required targets and benchmarking procedures.

6.1 Latency targets (hosted API)
- Text generation (small-medium models <25B): p50 <= 80ms, p95 <= 400ms, p99 <= 800ms for single-token continuation on a 32-token request baseline (baseline depends on model class).
- Large models and multi-turn chat: publish model-specific profiles. Dedicated capacity may have tighter SLA guarantees per contract.

6.2 Throughput and batching
- Document baseline batch sizes and expected throughput for each model variant. Provide guidance on batching config and trade-offs for latency vs throughput.

6.3 Benchmarking and perf-suite
- Use standardized perf harness (see eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite) with reproducible inputs and pinned hardware. Report p50/p95/p99, GPU memory, and tokens/sec.
- Benchmarks must be run on release candidates for model or runtime changes that might affect latency or memory.

6.4 Capacity planning
- Maintain headroom for traffic spikes: target 40% spare capacity at region level under expected P99 load. Document autoscaling policies and burst capacity allowances.

6.5 Cost-performance tradeoffs
- Capture unit cost (cost per token) on model cards and in rollout notes. Use Redwood Optimize recommendations to select quantization, batching, and routing policies for workloads.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process
Intro: ADRs document important technical decisions that have broad impact. Use ADRs for API-breaking changes, infra model changes, and long-lived architectural trade-offs.

7.1 When to write an ADR
- Any decision that changes a public API, requires cross-team coordination, or materially affects reliability/cost.

7.2 ADR template (required fields)
- Title: short, descriptive.
- Status: proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded.
- Context: why the decision is needed.
- Decision: what was chosen.
- Consequences: short-term and long-term effects, migration steps.
- Owners: who is accountable.
- Date: decision date.

7.3 Review and publication
- ADRs must be reviewed by affected teams and an architecture review board (ARB) representative. Approved ADRs are published in confluence under architecture-and-standards and linked from service READMEs.

7.4 ADR lifecycle
- Revisit ADRs periodically (annually) or when they hinder progress. Use deprecation ADRs to supersede previous decisions.

8) Operational playbook and runbooks
- For each service and model: include health endpoints (/healthz, /ready), runbook actions for common alerts, escalation path (pager on-call -> service owner -> platform on-call), and rollback steps.
- Template: Problem, Impact, Detection, Mitigation, Rollback, Postmortem owner.

9) Ownership and governance
- Each standard in this document has an owner: Architecture & Standards (maintainers: eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime). Day-to-day ownership for service-specific deviations belongs to the service owner and must be documented in a recorded ADR or an approved exception in the risk-and-exceptions register.

Appendix A — SLO example table
| Service class     | Availability SLO  | Latency SLO (p95)      | Error budget policy | Notes |
|------------------|-------------------|-------------------------|----------------------|-------|
| Public-hosted API | 99.95%            | <= 400ms (small models) | 0.05% monthly        | Tiered SLAs for enterprise |
| Dedicated         | SLA-defined       | SLA-defined             | Contractual           | Per-customer configs |

Appendix B — Quick ADR example
- Title: Move inference routing to regional-first policy
- Status: accepted
- Context: global-first routing causes increased cross-region latency and bandwidth cost for multi-tenant workloads.
- Decision: route traffic to regional capacity by default, fallback to global pool when regional capacity is saturated.
- Consequences: requires changes to routing service, new metrics (regional_fallback_rate), and a migration plan for existing customers over 90 days.
- Owners: Eng Platform (Jordan Lee).
- Date: 2026-11-20

References and links
- eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture (design doc)
- eng-infra/terraform-and-iac bootstrap templates
- eval-harness and model-onboarding pages for evaluation and safety suite requirements

If you propose a deviation from these standards
1. Create an ADR describing the deviation and rationale.
2. Get reviewers from impacted teams and the ARB.
3. Request an exception in the risk-and-exceptions register if the deviation touches security/compliance.

Contact
- Architecture & Standards maintainers: eng-platform@redwood.example.com.
- For runtime/model-serving questions: eng-serving-runtime@redwood.example.com.

This document is intended to be a single source of truth. Keep it up-to-date and link to more detailed per-service docs and ADRs where needed.
